One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet 
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). The checker reaches walk's programs after the switch-over (P-12).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled run time"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, rea
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled run time" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1.
- F-19 **Implicit parallelism: a `for` loop is parallel unless every generator is `seq`, and a tuple's elements and an operator's operands are evaluated in parallel.** `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). No program under `explorations/` writes `spawn` or `also`. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayTy
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` cla
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is
- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes, so a division by zero ends the run (row 336). Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;

entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage with the full overloading check: the gate's distance/run.sh, with the
# shadowed OverloadingChecker (checker-shadow.py beside this script) compiled by scalac and
# put ahead of everything on the run's class path.
#
#     explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export] [catch]
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with the call set up as the fortress-repo skill says, after
# ant compileAll. With `export`, the export check's isDeclaredName admits symbolic names too;
# with `catch`, a checker crash on one name is printed and the check goes on (checker-shadow.py).
# The scratch directory gets the shadow source and classes, the copy of run.sh (whose one
# changed line puts $EXTRA_CP first on the java class path), and the run's own scratch
# (run.txt, errors.tsv) under <scratch-dir>/d.
set -u
OUT=${1:?usage: run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export]}
SC=${2:?usage: run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export]}
case "$SC" in /*) ;; *) SC="$PWD/$SC" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
P="$FH/explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2"
mkdir -p "$SC/ocsrc" "$SC/occlasses" || exit 1
rm -f "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala
rm -rf "$SC/occlasses"/* 
python3 "$P/checker-shadow.py" "$FH" "$SC/ocsrc" "${@:3}" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1)
java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -nowarn -classpath "$CP" -d "$SC/occlasses" -encoding UTF-8 \
     "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala || { echo "run-shadow: scalac failed" >&2 ; exit 1 ; }
sed 's#-cp "\$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:#-cp "${EXTRA_CP:+$EXTRA_CP:}$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:#' \
    "$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh" > "$SC/run.sh"
grep -q 'EXTRA_CP' "$SC/run.sh" || { echo "run-shadow: run.sh's class path line moved" >&2 ; exit 1 ; }
# run.sh finds its helpers through $FORTRESS_HOME, so the copy may live anywhere
EXTRA_CP="$SC/occlasses" bash "$SC/run.sh" "$OUT" "$SC/d"

#!/bin/bash
# seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
#
# Makes a worktree that is ready to compile and run Fortress without building anything, by copying the
# build and the caches of a baseline worktree that has been built once, and translating the parts of the
# caches that are keyed by the source tree's absolute path (explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md).
#
#   <base-worktree>  a clean worktree of this repository at some commit B, on which `ant compileAll` and the
#                    library-order recompile (explorations/repo-internals.md, "Compile order matters") have
#                    run, and nothing since.
#   <new-worktree>   where the new worktree goes; made by `git worktree add`, reused if it already exists.
#   <branch>         the branch it checks out: an existing local branch, else origin's, else a new branch
#                    cut from <start-point>, which defaults to B; `-` makes a detached worktree at
#                    <start-point> instead. Old-against-new runs need no copy of the base: tools/old-fortress.sh
#                    runs the base build itself with a private caches folder.
#
# What it does, in order: adds the worktree; copies ProjectFortress/build, ProjectFortress/.dependencies
# and default_repository/caches from the base; renames every file of the AST caches (analyzed_cache,
# interpreter_cache, interpreter_parsed_cache) to the hash of its source's new path (NamingCzar.deCaseName,
# compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-245; GraphNode.java:33 hashes the canonical path) and rewrites the base path
# inside it; rewrites the base path in the bytecode-cache jars' SourceFile attributes (debug information
# only: jars copied unchanged also run, but their stack traces would name the base's files); and makes the
# new worktree the base's replica in its file dates too. The copies keep the base's dates (cp -a), every
# tracked file whose content is the base's takes the base file's date, and every tracked file that differs
# from B, committed or not, is stamped later than everything copied. Dates decide three things. The
# repository uses a cached entry only when it is not older than its source (repository/GraphRepository.java:244,
# :283; a changed api also makes everything that imports it stale, :600-620). Ant regenerates the AST
# nodes, the parsers and Operators.java when an input is newer than the generated file (build.xml:371-384,
# :450-467, :1335-1400); the checkout's own dates make it regenerate them, and javac then recompiles 1,077
# files. And javac recompiles a source newer than its class (build-cache-exploration.md, section 6). So the
# next `fortress compile` of a differing library source rebuilds it, and a worktree whose ProjectFortress/src
# differs from B is seeded with a warning: the copied build is B's, so the worker runs ant compileAll, which
# recompiles the differing sources (and deletes the caches, build.xml:715 and :356), and the library-order
# recompile before its first compiled run. The base's own dates must be a build's: a base built in place by
# ant, or seeded by this script.
#
# A worktree that already has ProjectFortress/build is left alone (a relaunch keeps the worker's own build);
# SEED_FORCE=1 replaces its build and caches with the base's.
#
# Prints one line per step with its time, and the seeded worktree's path last. Exits non-zero, having

"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

- F-249 **Under walk, a program that imports only the prelude reaches the string objects' own `||` only through `String`'s abstract `opr ||(self, b:String)`.** The string objects' own `||` are those that the objects `FlatString` and `EmptyString` declare, and that the trait `Concatenable` declares for the objects `CatString` and `SubString`. Code inside `FortressLibrary` reaches `FlatString`'s own `||` directly, because `FortressLibrary` imports `FlatString`'s api, which declares it. This bears on one proposed change: to move `String`'s `||` members to top-level declarations over `(Any, String)` and `(String, Any)`, as the library declares `juxtaposition`. Their meet, the top-level declaration over `(String, String)` that the Meet Rule requires, must then delegate to the string objects' own `||`. `FortressLibrary`, where the meet is declared, sees those only where an api that it imports states them: `FlatString`'s api does, and the probe added five lines to `String.fsi` for `Concatenable`'s and `EmptyString`'s. # Rung B of climb batch 21: the skeptic's verdict

## 2. The diff

**The library** is the probe's `subscripts-index-bound.patch` with the three changes the report names: `trait Index extends Any end` with its own comment before `Indexed`'s (P-156; question 1), `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\] where { I extends Index }` in both files (question 2, its default and the curator's answer), and `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` (`Library/Random.fsi:260`, `.fss:374`), a file beyond the brief's whose `FullRange[\T\]` needs the bound; every caller in the tree passes `ZZ32`. The patch's 40 edits cover every generic declaration of `FortressLibrary` that instantiates an indexed type at its own parameter: the full check brings no bound error.

**The checker.** `pSubInner`'s new case (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:332-333`) and `pExcInner`'s (`:566-567`) are the probe's and the planner's cases with the qualified name and with `e1.nonEmpty`; the two sides agree (fork 7; the judgement, section 2, item 1(a)). The `Object` shortcut excepts `Index` (`:262`), so `Index <: Object` falls to the parents case, where `Index`'s one parent is `Any`. A tuple type against any other trait type, `ZZ32` included, still falls to the old cases and excludes it, as the revised sentence "A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than Any and Index" says. `isLibraryIndex` (`:853-862`) reads the api's name as `Types.immutableHeapSeqName()` builds its name from `fortressLibrary()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java:100-102`), the library's way.

**Walk.** `subtypeOf`, `meet` and `join` read the rule, `excludesOther` its dual, and `FType.excludesOther` asks the tuple when the trait is `Index` (`FType.java:205`). `FTypeVoid` extends `FTypeTuple` with an empty list and overrides only `excludesOther` (`FTypeVoid.java:17`, `:24-31`), so on the worker's head the void type took the rule: the defect of section 3, fixed.

**The desugarer.** The library's `Index` keeps `extends Any` (`PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:127-130`, `:169-171`); a clause naming only `Index` and `Any` gets `Object` beside `Index` (`:91-123`). This is the reading under which the revised traits chapter's sentence, "every trait except Any, Object and Index implicitly extends the trait Object", holds for a trait that extends only `Index`; no decision covers it and the worker put it to the curator. I agree with it. The bare text `Index` is read before names are bound; on the compiled path, whose library has no `Index`, a program's own `trait Index` and `object Slot extends Index` compile and run as on the old code (section 3).

**The specification.** The four passages and the Appendix I entry are in the S1 form. The entry quotes the Working Draft at the right lines (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:134-136`, `:215-216`, `:263-265`, `:272-273`; `traits.tex:181-183`, `:193-194`; `appendices/future.tex:200-207`) and `types.tick:341`, `:424`, does not call the rule the team's own fix, quotes the "magic to convert" and describes the two ways kept open. `future.tex`'s box has the form of the `revival-meet` box. I added two sentences to its Effect (section 4). My build of the specification (`cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex`): 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL' twice, and the strict grep of the log, `grep -c "LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|^! Undefined control sequence"`, prints 0.

**Where I differ from the worker's account.**
- Decision 7 keeps `()` out of the rule "in the checker", with "() is no index" as its evidence, and record.md's change said "`()` is no `Index`"; walk did not keep it out. My fix does, so the sentence now holds on both paths.

The qualified name matters on the compiled path and in the desugarer's reading; the decision stands.

With a second parameter it does, and walk then reads the dual as the checker does: `TupleIndexExclusionWalk`, section 3.

## 3. My programs, old against new

Programs under `tmp/rung-index-bound/skeptic/p/`, run with `bin/fortress P.fss` on the rung's build (private caches) and with `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base21 <tree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss` on the old code; the checker over a program with the interpreter's library by the count stage's driver, `java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=<fresh> -cp "<count scratch>/head/classes:$CP" WorldFlip -stop typecheck P.fss`.

- **Overloads over `Index`, walk and checker.** `h(x: Index)` beside `h(x: (ZZ32, ZZ32))` and `g[\I extends Index\](x: I)` beside `g(x: (ZZ32, ZZ32))`: walk 'h index pair index', 'g generic index pair generic index'; the checker accepts both pairs and refuses only `h((i, i, i))` (NEW-B-1). `k(x: Index)` beside `k(x: Foo)`, a trait of the program's own: walk refuses, 'first parameters x:[Foo] and x:[Index] are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present', as it refuses `k(x: Bar)` beside `k(x: Foo)` on the old and the new code.

This is the test of walk's exclusion that no test held: `TupleIndexExclusionWalk`.

**Fix (defect), `e39d5b08d`, settled: walk's tuple rule leaves out the void type.**

(** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts
    to String and concatenates **)
opr ||(a:Any, b:String):String = ("" || a) || b
opr ||(a:String, b:String):String =
    typecase a of
        a':FlatString => a' || b
        a':Concatenable => a' || b
        else => concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(a, b)
    end
opr ||(a:String, b:Any):String = a || cast[\Object\](b).asString

(** The operator %|||% with at least one String argument converts to string,
    then appends with a whitespace separator unless one of the two arguments is
    empty.  If there is an empty argument, the other argument is returned. **)
opr |||(a:Any, b:String): String = (""||a) ||| b
opr |||(a:String, b:String): String =

content.content:
# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.

## When the text and an implementation disagree

- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.

## Citing it

- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

content.content:
- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). When it landed, the distance stage's self-type class fell from 29 errors to 0 (the distance from 85 to 55), one measurement on that tree. Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]`: an open defect (row 695). The rule refuses, rightly, two team declarations, each an open row: the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator` (row 710) and `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7.
- F-227 **The compiled checker replaces a closed trait among an intersection's conjuncts by those of its listed types that no other conjunct excludes, only where that excluding conjunct names no type variable or inference variable, so `K ∩ R[\T\]` stays as written; below a union, an inference variable takes the whole union as one upper bound, and a type variable is tried through its bound as well as against each member.** The code is `normConjunct` and, for the union cases, `pSubInner`, in `scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`. So a call through a parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound that excludes one of its listed types checks, and a generic declaration so bounded, beside a declaration on the closed trait, is a valid overloading (rows 686, 687, 689, 690 and 711). A call whose argument's type only carries the parameter, `Box[\T\]`, under a ground second bound, stays refused: an open defect (row 712). Before the checker kept such an intersection as written, it accepted, through the expansion, an overloading that it now refuses, on a question that Appendix I lists as not settled (row 713, contested; `compiler_tests/XXXOverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion` pins the refusal). Gated by `compiler_tests/*TwoBoundsClosedTrait` and `*TwoGroundBounds*ClosedTrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
- F-258 **Walk and the compiled checker read exclusion between two declarations, one or both with static parameters, over the whole parameter type, by existential reduction.** A value of both declared domains has, at each position, one instance of each generic type that the two parameter types there are or extend, so those instances' static arguments are equal; the two domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where, at the instance they force, the parameter types at some position exclude. Walk: the Meet branches of `genericPairValid` and of `validOnDeclaredDomains`'s generic-beside-plain reading also ask `domainsExcludeTogether` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:935` at `a93fb3bfd`), which reads bounds where `mayBeEqual` and `meetParams` read them and reads no `where` clause, varargs or lists of different lengths; at the instance the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter apart only where they cannot meet at any instance of it: an object type apart from a type that neither it nor a supertype of it may be, and no `comprises` clause (`excludesAtMeet`, `OverloadedFunction.java:1041` at `84957e6ef`). The checker: `OverloadingOracle.excludes` asks `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.emptyED` beside `subtypeED` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:326`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:444`): the existential reduction's first premise alone, its bounds not read. On the interpreter's library `emptyED` is never reached: `subtypeED` shows all 691 meets the count stage tests empty. The two paths differ on two type parameters whose bounds exclude (row 786); on such a pair one of whose declarations has a `where` clause, which walk refuses and the checker accepts (row 787); and on a pair that walk's parameter check reads apart, reading an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type it is at some instance, as `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which walk loads and the checker refuses (row 788). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`, `GenericPairForcedObjectApartWalk`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/GenericPairExcludesTogether` and `GenericPairSharedSupertypeExclusion` (load, compile and dispatch), and `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairFreeArgumentWalk`, `GenericPairObjectSupertypeOverlapWalk` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXGenericPairFreeArgument` (refused). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` sections 2, 5 and 7.

- F-81 **In the interpreter's library, every Meet Rule pair inside one type that the compiled checker checks has a declaration on its meet. The checker skips operators whose names are symbols (row 584); checked, their pairs give the errors of F-245.** `String`'s juxtaposition is three top-level operators, since two functional methods with `self` at different positions have no meet. `String`'s `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///`, which paired `(a:Any, self)` with `(self, b:Any)`, the shape the specification refuses, are now three top-level operators each too (F-276). F-245's measurement found other pairs without a meet, among them `Indexed`'s three subscripts in 17 types. The rung that added these meets also set the declared types listed in report section 1 to what their bodies answer. Elsewhere in the library some still differ, such as `__bigOperator2`'s fused branch (F-85). Gated by `tests/LibraryMeetDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-245 **Checking symbolic operators for overloading adds 186 errors to the distance in the compiled checker, measured at `d97001d19`, whose code is climb batch 20's gate, with crashes caught per name: 54 are cleared by known library fixes (F-276), 8 by the exclusion test that P-157 decides (F-277), and 124 wait on P-156's index bound.** As the stage runs, the 186 are 185 errors and three crashes on `||`, in `List`'s api and component and `String`'s component, "E is not in the kind env": a checker crash that no fix or design clears (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` section 1.3). The check was turned on in a copy of the checker whose three loops admit every operator; the checker as built skips them (row 584). On climb batch 21's base the stage gives 191, the distance's 5 and these 186 (`compile-ladder/plan-21/probes/full-check-base.tsv`), 137 with the known fixes alone, and 183 with the exclusion test alone. The two designs: a bound on the subscripts' index type (124 errors), and a vector plus a number beside a vector plus a vector (8). The probe's candidates S1, an index bound with a rule for tuple indices, and A2, `Vector` and `Matrix` leaving `AdditiveGroup`, clear them with nothing new; A3, the scalar `+` and `-` dropped, also clears the 8. The largest families are the subscripts over a generic `Indexed` (124) and `String`'s four concatenation operators, `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///` (40). An earlier measurement, at `d212b2c1f`, counted 205; batches since cleared `FlatString`'s pair (2; F-259) and 20 of the 21 `^` errors (F-263), and added 3: `|_|` 1 and the scalar `+` and `-` 2. Walk's meet check, which also skips symbolic operators and judges neither `String`'s pairs, the subscripts, `^` nor `=`, refused only `EmptyString`'s `||` when widened the same way in the first probe of these operators. Detail: `perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` sections 0 to 2; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` section 1.5.
- F-259 **An object or trait whose `extends` clause names `Any` alone is an `Object` on both paths, and such an object expression under walk, and `String`'s two top-level `||` over `Any` convert by the library's own way.** The pre-disambiguation desugaring that both paths run gives such a clause `{Object}`, as it gives an empty one, and leaves `Any`'s and `Object`'s own declarations as written. `opr ||(a:Any, b:String)` is `("" || a) || b` and `opr ||(a:String, b:Any)` is `a || cast[\Object\](b).asString` (top-level since F-276); `FlatString`'s api states its component's header, with no `opr ||(a:FlatString, self)`. \TYP{Object}.
A trait that extends \TYP{Index} and no other trait but \TYP{Any}

We define the extension relation to be the transitive closure
of implicit and
explicit extension.
That is, trait \VAR{T} \emph{extends} trait \VAR{U}

relation satisfying these conditions.

rooted at the traits \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}.

content.content: (Bash completed with no output)

- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. A tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`, on both paths and in the specification: a typing rule that changes no value, so `m[i, j]` passes its tuple `(i, j)` as before. Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question, and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header. `Index` stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`: it is declared `trait Index extends Any`, which the desugaring and walk keep as written and the traits chapter names as an exception to the rule that every trait extends `Object`, so a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, and P-42's tuples stay out of `Object`, as the specification's `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` keeps them. `BoundedRange`, which cannot take the bound, since the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56), keeps its narrowed `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` under the method condition `where { I extends Index }`, the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only; after the switch-over the code generator's refusal of a method with a `where` clause stops it too, as it stops `SumReduction`'s two `distribute`s (row 701). Row 783: the subscript pair.

# Climb batch 21: the gather's record

Written at the gather stage of climb batch 21's first run (2026-10-23), the run of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-21.md` (rungs S, B, X and N), on `main` from the base `00f2e1bdc5350b7590e4179e1b04bf6580d915f3`. `main` was at the base when the gather began, and no other commit came to it while the gather worked. Every rung was approved by its skeptic, with no contested fix, no judge and no repair round. No branch is a parent of anything on `main`, and each branch stays as it is: `wip/rung-symbolic-library` at `42653e89b`, `wip/rung-index-bound` at `135c013c1`, `wip/rung-self-type-exclusion` at `101ade40d`, `wip/rung-slices-list-equality` at `33fb2f720`.

**Preconditions.** `git status --porcelain` printed nothing, and `00f2e1bdc` is an ancestor of `HEAD` (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`, exit 0). `ledger.py landing-check 00f2e1bdc` on the base printed "no finding".

**Scratch.** The patches are `tmp/gather/<slug>.patch` in the main tree, each `git diff 00f2e1bdc...<branch>`. One tree was seeded outside the main tree from the batch's base build, `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base21 /home/user/fortress-gather21 wip/gather-21 00f2e1bdc5350b7590e4179e1b04bf6580d915f3` ("seeded from /home/user/fortress-base21 (aa5ff2423) in 5 s"; the base build's code is the base's, its commit differing only under `explorations/`). Nothing was built or run in the main tree or in the base build. In the gather tree the four patches were first applied together, in the order below, with `git apply --3way --index` (no conflict), and built: `ant compileAll` ("Caches /home/user/fortress-gather21/default_repository/caches started again, empty", "BUILD SUCCESSFUL", "Total time: 45 seconds"), then the library order (five compiles, each `rc=0`, five jars in `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`). The closing tests ran there (below). The tree was then reset to the base and the four rung commits were composed there one by one, on the local branch `wip/gather-21`, each folding its rung's record; `main` was fast-forwarded to them (`git merge --ff-only wip/gather-21`), so their hashes are the gather tree's, and the closes and this record were committed on `main` itself (gather.3: no rung's staged change sat in `main`'s index while a record was folded, as one did at climb batch 20). The code and tests the closing tests ran on are `main`'s: the four patches applied to the base in a scratch index, `git diff --stat <that tree> ff19305cc -- Library ProjectFortress build.xml bin`, prints nothing.

## The landed commits

| Order | Rung | Branch | Commit on `main` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | S, `rung-symbolic-library` | `wip/rung-symbolic-library` at `42653e89b` | `557cabb04` |
| 2 | X, `rung-self-type-exclusion` | `wip/rung-self-type-exclusion` at `101ade40d` | `64fa505c4` |
| 3 | B, `rung-index-bound` | `wip/rung-index-bound` at `135c013c1` | `153887360` |
| 4 | N, `rung-slices-list-equality` | `wip/rung-slices-list-equality` at `33fb2f720` | `ff19305cc` |
| | the rows' closes | | `b169d1fbd` |

## The order the rungs were applied in

S, X, B, N. No rung declares `landsOnlyWith`, so the first rule orders nothing. The files the rungs share (`comm -12` of the lists `git diff --name-only 00f2e1bdc...<branch>`), with each rung's lowest edited line from the hunk headers of `git diff -U0 00f2e1bdc...<branch>`:

| File | S | B | X | N | Order by the lowest line |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` | 452 (`Integral`'s `=`) | 533 (`ZZ32`'s header) | | | S, B |
| `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` | 702 (`Integral`'s `=`) | 729 (`ZZ32`) | | 2732 (`Array2.subarray`) | S, B, N |
| `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` | | 4062 (the new entry) | 2852 ("Overloading with static parameters") | 160 ("Conditional extension") | N, X, B |

S shares no file with X, so that pair keeps the manifest's order, S before X. B and N are ordered both ways, B first by `FortressLibrary.fss` and N first by `changes.tex`, so that pair keeps the manifest's order, B before N. The other pairs that share a file are each ordered by `changes.tex` alone: N before X and X before B. With B before N these make a cycle (B, N, X, B), so no order keeps every pair. The gather kept the two pairs the rule fixes outright and the manifest's order for the rest, and broke the pair whose cost is least: S, X, B, N keeps S before B and N, S before X, B before N and X before B, and breaks N before X. The alternative that keeps `changes.tex` whole, S, N, X, B, breaks the manifest's B before N; S, B, N, X breaks X before B, and X's 43 lines in `changes.tex` would then move B's entry where N's 11 do now. forCurator: The order is S, X, B, N, not the batch record's S, B, X, N. That order rested on X sharing no file with the other rungs (explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-21.md:41), but X, B and N all edit Specification/appendices/changes.tex (lowest edited lines: N :160, X :2852, B :4062). The role's rule then orders the pairs in a cycle: B before N by the manifest, since the .fss and changes.tex order that pair both ways; N before X and X before B by changes.tex. The gather broke N before X, so N's 11 lines move X's and B's Appendix I lines (rung B's entry is at Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4123 on main). The folded record cites main's lines. Reversible, and nothing waits. Detail: explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-21/RECORD.md:19-35.
